paras: The whipping of Cyrus Davis was a whitecapping attack on a Black barber of Blackville, Barnwell County, South Carolina, who was carried into the country and flogged on the night of August 8, 1895. Davis survived, and he said he had been told the beating was punishment for his testimony as a witness in a murder case. Papers in South Carolina called it an outrage, while New York papers reported it as part of a wave of whitecapping in the county.

Davis had been a witness for the State in a murder case that, according to the Blackville correspondent, had drawn a great deal of interest, and his evidence was said to have been given at the second trial. A Charleston dispatch said such outrages had been going on for more than a year in that part of Barnwell County, and that the band had more often chosen white victims than Black ones.

A party came to Davis's home at night and told him he was wanted to shave a dead man, and he set out with them in a vehicle. Once in the country, a crocus sack was thrown over his head and he was severely whipped. The later Charleston dispatch added that he was also beaten, that lighted matches were applied to his wounds, and that he was left lying in the woods all night until he was found the next morning and carried home.

The Blackville correspondent reported that Davis "looked rather badly bruised" the morning after. Davis said he was told he was whipped for his evidence against a man charged with murder, while the Charleston version, introduced with "It is said," gave the reason as having "swore falsely" as a State witness in the Court of Sessions.

The Blackville chief of police had heard of the whipping but had received no official report, and it had taken place outside the town. The Charleston dispatch reported that thirty suspects had been arrested over the Barnwell whitecapping, several of whom claimed alibis, though it did not connect the arrests to the Davis case. A few days later, A. H. Patterson of Barnwell told Governor Evans that there was no organized band of white-caps in the county and that each reported case stood "on their own bottom." No report of a prosecution for the attack on Davis appears in the coverage.

The first report was a special from Blackville to the Charleston News and Courier, which ran in the Sumter Watchman and Southron on August 14, the Winnsboro News and Herald on August 15 and the Union Times on August 23 under the headline "An Outrage in Barnwell." That story described Davis as "a colored barber," called the attack an "outrage," and closed by suggesting the right persons could find the culprits and "have the law take its proper course."

On August 17 the New-York Tribune and The Sun printed a Charleston dispatch that called Davis's treatment "inhuman" and said earlier news gave only a "meagre" idea of the facts. That dispatch framed the whitecapping as a concern because settlers from Pullman, Illinois, were expected to move to the county, and it paired Davis with George Carroll, a white man whitecapped on a Monday night that same week. The Sun headed the story "Inhuman Treatment of a Negro and a White Man and His Family" and stressed that there was "no political feature," while the Tribune's headline spoke only of a man shot at "for being unsociable," which referred to Carroll.
No report of the whipping was found in the Black press.

Accounts differ on details: the Blackville special mentions only a hooded whipping, while the Charleston dispatch adds burning with matches and a night left in the woods. His name also appears as "Cyrus David" in the Sumter paper, "Cyrus Davis" in the Winnsboro reprint and the Tribune, and "Circus Davis" in The Sun.

reader.title: Whipping of Cyrus Davis
bases: A band the Charleston dispatch called 'White Caps' took Davis from his home at night and flogged him as punishment for his court testimony (A1, A3, A4).

Two separate South Carolina dispatches, the Blackville special of Aug. 9 (A1, A2) and the Charleston special of Aug. 16 (A3, A4), agree that Davis, a Black barber, was carried off at night and severely whipped for his testimony, though both may trace to News and Courier correspondents.

accounts.label: Blackville special to the News and Courier
accounts.gist: Davis was lured from home on the pretext of shaving a dead man, hooded with a sack and severely flogged; he said he was told it was for his evidence against a man charged with murder.

accounts.label: Charleston special, Aug. 16
accounts.gist: White Caps whipped and beat Davis, put lighted matches to his wounds and left him in the woods overnight; 'it is said' he was told it was for swearing falsely as a State witness.

accounts.label: A. H. Patterson of Barnwell
accounts.gist: There was no organized band of white-caps in Barnwell; each reported case stood on its own.

framing.detail: Headlined 'An Outrage in Barnwell' with the subhead 'A Witness in a Murder Case Kidnapped and Whipped,' and closed by saying the right persons could find the culprits and 'have the law take its proper course.'

The Charleston dispatch called Davis's treatment 'inhuman' and the outrages 'gross violations of the law,' framing them as a concern for planned settlement from Pullman, Ill.; the Tribune's headline featured only the white victim Carroll.

set_aside: Columbia, Aug. 17: Barnwell whitecaps drove H. H. Nevins's hands from his place; governor ordered Sheriff Lancaster to investigate. Davis not named.
Editorial note: white caps in Barnwell persecuting farmer Nevins; calls for prison terms. Davis not mentioned.

Letter from a Barnwell Black man asking the governor for protection from 'white caps'; a Black man tied and beaten weeks earlier, described as the case already referred to Sheriff Lancaster (apparently the Nevins matter).
